# Anonymous Submissions store no person and no time, and are unlinkable at rest, not against a restore

**Threat model.** The Lead, Organization admins, and anyone using the product (UI, API, exports) must never be able to link a member to their Submission, and neither can an operator reading stored data, dumps, or R2 backups. We do **not** claim to defend against an operator who restores the Durable Object to a past moment (point-in-time recovery replays every write, including the one transaction that writes a Participation record and its Submission), reads Cloudflare's internal edge logs, or changes the code to start logging. Against that we use controls instead: only named people can trigger a restore, the privacy page states the 30-day restore window, and code changes on the submission path need review. The answer page's "Your name is never stored with your answers" is true of everything stored.

**Design.**
- Everything lives in the Organization's Durable Object. There is no per-Round object. The first Answer writes the Participation record and a Submission holding that one Answer in **one transaction**, which is how a double submission is rejected (a unique Participation record per Round and Person).
- An anonymous Submission stores only its Round, its Answers, and an Edit key hash. It stores **no person, no Invitation, and no time at all**, not even the day SPEC allows. A Participation record stores Round, Person, and the fact of answering, also with no time.
- Submission and Answer tables are `WITHOUT ROWID` with random 128-bit keys. Reads aggregate or sort by the random key. Dumps and backups are written in key order.
- **The anonymous Submission table has no person column, ever.** Attributed Submissions get their own table, so no bug can put a name on an anonymous answer.
- The Invitation token travels in the **URL fragment**, so the answer page GET (and every link scanner) never sends it. The page POSTs it to a **separate Submission Worker** with logs, traces, tail, Logpush, and Analytics Engine writes all off. That Worker logs error codes only. Tokens are stored only as hashes.
- The **browser generates the Edit key** and sends only its SHA-256 hash with the first Answer. Later Answers and changes carry only the Edit key. **No request may carry both an Invitation token and an Edit key**, and the server rejects one that does.

## Considered Options

- **Submissions in a separate Durable Object.** Rejected: without one transaction, a crash either loses the Answer or allows a second Submission, and the timing gap still exists.
- **Shuffled batch writes.** Rejected: buffered Answers are lost if the object is evicted, and it defends only against the restore threat we don't claim to cover.
- **A nullable person column shared with attributed mode.** Rejected: a single bug would put names on anonymous answers.

## Consequences

Response and answer counts come from Participation records. Answer latency is measured only in tests on a preview stage. Deleting a Person deletes their Participation records, and their anonymous Submissions survive. A member who loses the Edit key cannot change their answers, and that is accepted.
# Comments are redacted when stored, and the raw text is never kept

Release 1's rule-based redaction (ADR 0001) runs in the Submission Worker as the comment is saved. It uses the Organization's roster at that moment, and only the redacted text is stored. The raw text exists only in that request's memory. It is never logged, stored, or sent to a model. We rejected keeping the raw text and redacting each time a comment is shown, for two reasons. Deleting a Person would take their name out of the roster and expose it in every old comment that mentions them. And raw comments at rest would be the most identifying data SurveyBeat holds.

**What is removed:**
- first names, last names, full names, and email local parts of every Person in the Organization, matched as whole words, ignoring case, width, and accents (names shorter than 2 characters are ignored);
- email addresses, phone numbers (7 or more digits with common separators), @handles, and every URL.

Each match becomes a placeholder (`[name]`, `[email]`, `[phone]`, `[handle]`, `[link]`). A comment is never held back as a whole. Roster names that are also ordinary words ("will", "may") are redacted anyway.

## Consequences

- Redaction is permanent. A false positive can't be undone, and a member who edits their comment edits the redacted text.
- People added to the roster later are not redacted from older comments.
- No nicknames, no names outside the roster, and no "unusual identifying phrases" in Release 1. The answer page says exactly what is and isn't removed.
- The Release 2 AI pass can only ever run on new comments, because the raw text of older comments no longer exists.

# What Cloudflare logs about a Worker request by default

Research for issue #10 (map #1). Throwaway branch, not for merging. Researched 2026-11-07 against developers.cloudflare.com and cloudflare.com.

**Why it matters.** SPEC §5.3 says request logs for the Submission endpoint must not contain the Invitation token, the Person, or the IP address together with the Submission. SPEC §6.4 sends errors and traces to Workers Logs and Workers Observability. SPEC §7 makes "logs from the submission path contain no identifiers" a release-blocking test. (The ticket also names GLOSSARY.md, but that file does not exist on `origin/main` yet.)

## TL;DR

1. **The default is on.** New Workers have `observability.enabled = true`, and `head_sampling_rate` defaults to 1. Every request gets an *invocation log*, labelled `Fetch <METHOD> <URL>`, with the full URL including the query string. The log also holds request and response metadata that Cloudflare does not fully document. Paid plans keep these logs for 7 days, the Free plan for 3.
2. **Traces are opt-in** (`observability.traces.enabled`). Once on, the inbound span records `url.full`, the full user agent, `cloudflare.ray_id`, ASN, and geo down to city. D1 and Durable Object SQL spans record `db.query.text`. The docs list no client IP attribute on spans.
3. **Tail Workers, `wrangler tail` and Logpush trace events carry `event.request.url` and `headers`.** Cloudflare's docs describe redaction only for the `tail()` handler. There it covers a fixed list of header names and ID-shaped substrings of the URL. `cf-connecting-ip` and `x-forwarded-for` are **not** on that list, and `getUnredacted()` bypasses all of it.
4. **The edge always writes an HTTP request log line**, with `ClientIP`, `ClientRequestURI` (path plus query) and `RayID`. A customer cannot stop the edge from writing it. A customer can only choose not to retain it (Logpull, off by default, 3 to 7 days) or not to push it (Logpush). Cloudflare publishes no fixed retention period for its own internal copy.
5. **Analytics Engine records only what `writeDataPoint` writes**, and keeps it 3 months. AI Gateway logs prompts and responses **by default**. Turnstile processes the client IP, TLS fingerprint and user agent.
6. **Design consequence.** Never put the Invitation token in the Submission URL. Send it in the POST body, or better, exchange it in an earlier request for a short-lived, unlinkable submission credential. Serve the Submission endpoint from its own Worker with `invocation_logs = false`, traces off, no `tail_consumers` and `logpush = false`. Sampling is per Worker or per environment, not per route. Test the result empirically, because Cloudflare does not publish the full field list of an invocation log.

## 1. Workers Logs (persisted logs)

Source: <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/workers-logs/>

- **Default on.** "Newly created Workers have it on by default." The `observability.enabled` key is shorthand for `logs.enabled`, "defaults to `true` for all new Workers", and makes the logs persist ([Wrangler configuration](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/configuration/)).
- **Invocation log.** "Each Workers invocation returns a single invocation log that contains details such as the Request, Response, and related metadata". These logs are identified by `$cloudflare.$metadata.type = "cf-worker-event"`. Each one is "enriched with information available to Cloudflare in the context of the invocation". A fetch invocation is shown as `Fetch <Method> <URL>`, so **the URL, query string included, is in the log**.
- **Request ID and Ray ID.** The Observability API schema defines `rayId` as the "Cloudflare Ray ID from the cf-ray header of the request that triggered the invocation", and `requestId` as the ID "that ties all logs from a single invocation together" ([API reference](https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/workers/subresources/observability/)). Each event also carries timestamps and duration (`$metadata.endTime` and `duration`), plus the account and service.
- **Not documented.** Cloudflare does not publish the complete field list of an invocation log. In particular, it does not say whether request headers or the `cf` object are stored, or whether redaction applies. Treat both as **unknown until verified** (see section 9).
- **Custom logs.** Every `console.log` line is stored and linked to the invocation by `requestId` and `rayId`. So any value logged on the Submission path ends up in the same log group as the URL and the Ray ID.
- **Turning it off or down:**
  ```toml
  [observability]
  enabled = true          # false = do not persist logs for this Worker
  head_sampling_rate = 1  # 0..1, per Worker, default 1

  [observability.logs]
  invocation_logs = false # keep console.log output, drop the automatic invocation log
  ```
  Per-environment overrides go under `[env.<name>.observability]`, and `observability` is an inheritable key. **There is no per-route setting.** Sampling is head-based per request: "When a request is sampled, all logs for that request are kept." Above the daily limit, Cloudflare applies a 1% head sample for the rest of the day.
- **Retention.** 3 days on Free, 7 days on Paid ("the stated maximum"). The maximum log size is 256 KB, and larger logs are truncated with `$cloudflare.truncated = true`.

## 2. Workers Observability: traces

Sources: <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/traces/>, <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/traces/spans-and-attributes/>

- **Opt-in.** Turn traces on with `[observability.traces] enabled = true`. The docs say that `observability.enabled = true` "currently enables logs only, not traces". `head_sampling_rate` takes 0 to 1 and defaults to 1 once traces are on. Logs and traces can use different sampling rates. Traces are kept for 7 days.
- **Inbound fetch handler span:** `http.request.method`, `url.full`, `url.path`, `network.protocol.name`, `http.request.header.accept`, `accept-encoding`, `accept-language`, `user_agent.original` plus parsed browser, OS and device fields, `cloudflare.asn`, `cloudflare.verified_bot_category`, `geo.timezone`, `geo.continent.code`, `geo.country.code`, `geo.locality.name`, `geo.locality.region`. The root span also gets `cloudflare.ray_id`, and all spans get `cloudflare.colo`.
- **No IP attribute is listed** on any span.
- **Outbound fetch spans** record `url.full`, `url.query`, `server.address`, a few content headers, and the body sizes.
- **Binding spans.** D1 and Durable Object SQL spans record **`db.query.text`**. If the SQL is parameterized, the text holds `?` placeholders, but string-interpolated values would end up in the trace. KV spans record the keys (`cloudflare.kv.query.keys`). A token used as a KV or D1 lookup key would therefore show up in the trace of the lookup request. Durable Object spans record `cloudflare.durable_object.id`.
- **Privacy reading.** Even without an IP, the combination of `url.full`, the full user agent, ASN, city, Ray ID and timestamp is close to identifying for a small team. In the Submission Worker, turn traces off.

## 3. Real-time logs (`wrangler tail`, dashboard Live view)

Source: <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/real-time-logs/>

- Real-time logs exist only while someone is tailing: "Real-time logs does not store Workers Logs." Each event is JSON with `outcome`, `scriptName`, `exceptions`, `logs`, `eventTimestamp`, and `event.request.{url, method, headers, cf}`.
- Anyone with access to the account can tail any Worker at any time, so this is an access-control concern rather than a retention one. The page does not say whether `wrangler tail` applies the redaction from section 4.

## 4. Tail Workers

Sources: <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/tail-workers/>, <https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/tail/>

- **Opt-in** per producer, through `tail_consumers`. That key is not inheritable, so each environment declares its own.
- A Tail Worker receives the same shape of event: request `url`, `method`, `headers` and `cf` (`IncomingRequestCfProperties`), plus logs, exceptions and diagnostics-channel events.

When using AI through OpenRouter, whether via the chat interface or the API, your prompts and responses go through multiple touchpoints. You control how your data is handled at each step.

This page gives an overview of how your data is stored and used by OpenRouter. More information is available in the [privacy policy](https://openrouter.ai/privacy) and [terms of service](https://openrouter.ai/terms).

OpenRouter does not store your prompts or responses, *unless* you opt in to one or both of the following, or content is flagged as potential CSAM:

### Training on Prompts

Each provider on OpenRouter has its own data handling policies. We reflect those policies in structured data on each AI endpoint that we offer.

On your account settings page, you can set whether you would like to allow routing to providers that may train on your data (according to their own policies). There are separate settings for paid and free models.

Wherever possible, OpenRouter works with providers to ensure that prompts will not be trained on, but there are exceptions. # Zero Data Retention

> How OpenRouter gives you control over your data

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Planned update (October 27, 2026):** OpenRouter will screen all inference requests, including ZDR traffic, for child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in flight. Content flagged as potential CSAM may be retained for human review, reporting, and preservation where required by law. This does not permit general retention or use for model training. [Read the announcement](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/csam-screening). We're updating this page and our related terms.

Zero Data Retention (ZDR) means no routine storage of prompts or responses after processing, apart from the CSAM exception described on this page.

## Data policy tiers

OpenRouter describes every endpoint's data policy with three tiers:

| Tier | What it means | Is your data trained on? |
| - | - | - |
| **ZDR** | No routine storage after processing, as described on this page. | No |
| **Safety Retention** | OpenRouter or a provider may retain prompts and responses from any request, whether flagged or not, only to detect, investigate, and prevent abuse. | No |
| **Retention and Training** | Data may be stored and used for training under the applicable provider policy. | May be, under the provider's policy |

Safety Retention limits why data can be kept. It does not require a request to be flagged before it can be stored.

## Allowing or excluding Safety Retention

When ZDR is enforced in your privacy settings or a guardrail, you choose whether Safety Retention endpoints are also allowed. The choice is separate for **Google** models and **All other models**, the two groups where Safety Retention endpoints exist today.

* **Allow Safety Retention:** ZDR-enforced requests can use ZDR endpoints and Safety Retention endpoints.
* **ZDR only:** ZDR-enforced requests use ZDR endpoints only. Safety Retention endpoints are excluded, so some models may be unavailable.

Set this in your [privacy settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy) or in a guardrail's settings. A guardrail can only be stricter than your account setting: if your account is set to ZDR only, a guardrail can't allow Safety Retention. If you haven't chosen, self-serve accounts allow Safety Retention and enterprise accounts use ZDR only.

In the API, `zdr: true` on a request follows the same account and guardrail choice. The guardrail fields are `allow_safety_retention_google` and `allow_safety_retention_other` in the [Guardrails API](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/guardrails/create-a-guardrail.md).

When ZDR isn't enforced, Safety Retention endpoints are available like any other endpoint that doesn't train on your data.

OpenRouter has [privacy settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy) that, when enabled, only allow you to route to endpoints that have a Zero Data Retention policy. You can enforce ZDR globally, per model group, per guardrail, or per request.

Providers that do not retain your data are also unable to train on your data. However we do have some endpoints & providers who do not train on your data but *do* retain it (e.g. to scan for abuse or for legal reasons). OpenRouter gives you controls over both of these policies.

> ZDR enforcement only applies to provider routing for inference requests. It does not apply to [plugins](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/plugins.md) and tools you choose to enable, such as [web search](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/web-search.md). These may be operated by third-party services with their own data retention policies. Review the data policies of any plugins or tools you enable if you have strict data retention requirements.

> One tool-level rule applies: when ZDR is enforced in your account privacy settings or a guardrail, the Web Search and Web Fetch server tools and the Web Search plugin reject the Firecrawl engine. See [Privacy and regional availability](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools.md#privacy-and-regional-availability) for each server tool's execution path and backend policy.

## How OpenRouter Manages Data Policies

OpenRouter works with providers to understand each of their data policies and structures the policy data in a way that gives you control over which providers you want to route to.

Note that a provider's general policy may differ from the specific policy for a given endpoint. OpenRouter keeps track of the specific policy for each endpoint, works with providers to keep these policies up to date, and in some cases creates special agreements with providers to ensure data retention or training policies that are more privacy-focused than their default policies.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If OpenRouter is not able to establish or ascertain a clear policy for a provider or endpoint, we take a conservative stance and assume that the endpoint both retains and trains on data and mark it as such.

A full list of providers and their data policies can be found [here](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/privacy/provider-logging.md#data-retention--logging). Note that this list shows the default policy for each provider; if there is a particular endpoint that has a policy that differs from the provider default, it may not be available if "ZDR Only" is enabled.

## Per-Model-Group ZDR Enforcement

Rather than a single global toggle, OpenRouter lets you enforce ZDR independently for different model groups. This is available in both your [account-level privacy settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy) and in [guardrails](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails.md).

The five model group scopes are:

| Model group | Effect when enabled |
| - | - |
| **Anthropic** | Removes first-party Anthropic endpoints (Bedrock and Vertex remain available) |
| **OpenAI** | Removes first-party OpenAI endpoints (Azure remains available) |
| **Google** | Removes AI Studio endpoints. Vertex endpoints that use Safety Retention remain available only if Safety Retention is allowed (see [Google Safety Retention](#google-safety-retention)) |
| **SpaceXAI** | Removes non-ZDR SpaceXAI endpoints (the ZDR SpaceXAI endpoint remains available) |
| **All other models** | Removes all other non-ZDR endpoints |

> [!TIP]
>
> **When to use per-model-group ZDR**
>
> Per-model-group ZDR is useful when you only need ZDR enforcement for certain model groups. For example, you may want to enforce ZDR for all other models while keeping first-party Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google endpoints available without the ZDR restriction.

### Account-level settings

In your [privacy settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy), each model group has its own toggle. Enabling a scope restricts all your requests to ZDR endpoints for that model group.

### Guardrail-level settings

When creating or editing a [guardrail](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails.md), you can set ZDR independently for each model group. This lets you apply different ZDR policies to different API keys or organization members.

In the API, these are represented as separate fields on the guardrail object:

| Field | Description |
| - | - |
| `enforce_zdr_anthropic` | Enforce ZDR for Anthropic endpoints |
| `enforce_zdr_openai` | Enforce ZDR for OpenAI endpoints |
| `enforce_zdr_google` | Enforce ZDR for Google endpoints |
| `enforce_zdr_xai` | Enforce ZDR for SpaceXAI endpoints |
| `enforce_zdr_other` | Enforce ZDR for all other model endpoints |

> [!NOTE]
>
> The legacy `enforce_zdr` field is deprecated. When provided, its value is copied into any per-model-group fields that are not explicitly set on the request. Use the per-model-group fields directly for new integrations.

## Google Safety Retention

Starting October 18, 2026, Google requires Safety Retention for Google models served through Vertex. With Safety Retention, Google doesn't retain prompts by default, but it may retain prompts that its safety classifiers flag, for up to 90 days, for abuse monitoring. Google doesn't use retained prompts for training. These endpoints don't meet a strict Zero Data Retention requirement.

When you enforce ZDR for Google models, you choose how OpenRouter treats these endpoints in your [privacy settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy) or on a guardrail:

| Choice | Effect |
| - | - |
| **ZDR only** | Excludes endpoints that use Safety Retention. Most Google models become unavailable. |
| **Allow Safety Retention** | Lets ZDR-enforced requests use endpoints that use Safety Retention. |

If you don't choose, enterprise accounts default to **ZDR only** and all other accounts default to **Allow Safety Retention**. On guardrails, use `allow_safety_retention_google` for Google models and `allow_safety_retention_other` for other models that use Safety Retention, such as open-weight models on Vertex. A guardrail can't allow Safety Retention when your account setting is **ZDR only**.

On a model page, the provider details for an endpoint that uses Safety Retention show **ZDR compatible: Only with Safety Retention allowed**.

If your own Google Cloud agreement includes zero data retention, you can use Vertex through your own key with **ZDR only**. Declare ZDR on your [BYOK](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md) key. Requests through that key are treated as ZDR. See [Declaring ZDR on a Key](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md#declaring-zdr-on-a-key).

## Per-Request ZDR Enforcement

In addition to account-level and guardrail-level settings, you can enforce Zero Data Retention on a per-request basis using the `zdr` parameter in your API calls.

The request-level `zdr` parameter operates as an "OR" with your account-wide and guardrail ZDR settings. If any is enabled, ZDR enforcement will be applied. This means the per-request parameter can only be used to ensure ZDR is enabled for a specific request, not to override or disable account-wide or guardrail enforcement.

This is useful for customers who don't want to globally enforce ZDR but need to ensure specific requests only route to ZDR endpoints.

### Usage

Include the `zdr` parameter in your provider preferences:

```json lines theme={null}
{
  "model": "gpt-4",
  "messages": [...],
  "provider": {
    "zdr": true
  }
}
```

When `zdr` is set to `true`, the request will only be routed to ZDR endpoints, plus Safety Retention endpoints if your settings allow them (see [Allowing or excluding Safety Retention](#allowing-or-excluding-safety-retention)). When `zdr` is `false` or not provided, ZDR enforcement still applies if enabled in your account or guardrail settings.

## ZDR with BYOK Keys

By default, a [BYOK](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md) key follows the same ZDR rules as OpenRouter credits. If your own provider agreement includes zero data retention, you can declare that on the key. ZDR enforcement then allows requests through that key even when the shared endpoint retains prompts. The declaration does not cover video generation. See [Declaring ZDR on a Key](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md#declaring-zdr-on-a-key).

## Caching

Some endpoints/models provide implicit caching of prompts. This keeps repeated prompt data in an in-memory cache in the provider's datacenter, so that the repeated part of the prompt does not need to be re-processed. This can lead to considerable cost savings.

OpenRouter has taken the stance that in-memory caching of prompts is *not* considered "retaining" data, and we therefore allow endpoints/models with implicit caching to be hit when a ZDR routing policy is in effect.

## ZDR for Private Endpoints

A [private endpoint](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/private-endpoints.md) connects a catalog model to a deployment you operate in your own provider account, authenticated with your [BYOK](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md) key. Only organizations granted private access can route to it. OpenRouter has no view into your agreement with that upstream, so the retention classification comes from a declaration you make when you create or edit the private endpoint.

### Declaration states

| Declaration | What it records | Routing when ZDR is required |
| - | - | - |
| **Not declared** | No statement about the upstream's retention. | Treated as retaining. The private endpoint is not eligible. |
| **Declared ZDR** | Your attestation that the upstream does not retain prompts or completions. | The private endpoint stays in your ZDR routing pool. |
| **Declared non-ZDR** | Your attestation that the upstream retains data. | Treated as retaining. The private endpoint is not eligible. |

"ZDR is required" means any enforcement path described above: the account-level privacy setting, a model-group or guardrail ZDR setting, or `provider.zdr` on the request.

### Not declared

A private endpoint does not inherit the data policy of any public endpoint or provider, even when it connects to the same upstream service. A new private endpoint with no declaration uses the conservative unverified fallback described in [How OpenRouter Manages Data Policies](#how-openrouter-manages-data-policies): OpenRouter treats it as retaining, so it is not eligible for any request that requires ZDR.

### Declared ZDR

Declaring ZDR keeps the private endpoint in your organization's ZDR routing pool. Every other routing constraint still applies: the requesting organization must hold private access to the endpoint, the endpoint must be available for the requested model, and provider preferences, guardrails, and other data-policy settings are evaluated as usual. The declaration only changes the retention classification. It does not add the private endpoint to the ZDR routing pool of any organization without private access, and it does not affect the ZDR eligibility of the public endpoints for the same model.

### Declared non-ZDR

Declaring non-ZDR records an explicit attestation that the upstream retains data. Under a ZDR requirement it routes the same way as **Not declared**. The difference is what your audit trail records: **Declared non-ZDR** is known and attested, **Not declared** is unknown.

### Existing private endpoints

A private endpoint created before this setting existed keeps its current classification and behaves as it did. Editing its declaration applies the rules above, subject to the override precedence below.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Overrides and attestations**
>
> An explicit OpenRouter data-policy override set by our team remains authoritative over your declaration. If OpenRouter has assigned a specific data policy to your private endpoint, that policy decides eligibility regardless of what you declared.
>
> A declaration is your attestation about your agreement with the upstream. OpenRouter records it and routes on it, and does not independently verify the upstream's contractual behavior.

## OpenRouter's Retention Policy

For inference content covered by OpenRouter's ZDR policy, we do not retain prompts or responses after processing, except when you explicitly choose to have us store them or when retention is needed for CSAM review, reporting, and related legal preservation. CSAM screening will also apply to requests covered by OpenRouter's ZDR policy. See [CSAM Screening Across OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/csam-screening).

The following endpoints are eligible when ZDR is enforced. Note that this list is also available programmatically via [https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr](https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr). It is automatically updated when there are changes to a provider's data policy. It also includes Safety Retention endpoints, which are used only if you [allow Safety Retention](#allowing-or-excluding-safety-retention). The [provider logging](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/privacy/provider-logging.md#data-retention--logging) table shows which providers use Safety Retention.

# Provider Routing

> Route requests to the best provider

OpenRouter routes requests to the best available providers for your model. By default, [OpenRouter routes each request](#default-routing) based on each provider's measured price, throughput, latency, and reliability.

You can customize how your requests are routed using the `provider` object in the request body for the [Responses API](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/overview.md) and [Chat Completions](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/chat/create-a-chat-completion.md).

The `provider` object can contain the following fields:

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `order` | string\[] | - | List of provider slugs to try in order (e.g. `["anthropic", "openai"]`). [Learn more](#ordering-specific-providers) |
| `allow_fallbacks` | boolean | `true` | Whether to allow backup providers when the primary is unavailable. [Learn more](#disabling-fallbacks) |
| `require_parameters` | boolean | `false` | Only use providers that support all parameters in your request. [Learn more](#requiring-providers-to-support-all-parameters) |
| `data_collection` | "allow" \| "deny" | "allow" | Control whether to use providers that may store data. [Learn more](#requiring-providers-to-comply-with-data-policies) |
| `zdr` | boolean | - | Restrict routing to only ZDR (Zero Data Retention) endpoints. [Learn more](#zero-data-retention-enforcement) |
| `enforce_distillable_text` | boolean | - | Restrict routing to only models that allow text distillation. [Learn more](#distillable-text-enforcement) |
| `only` | string\[] | - | List of provider slugs to allow for this request. [Learn more](#allowing-only-specific-providers) |
| `ignore` | string\[] | - | List of provider slugs to skip for this request. [Learn more](#ignoring-providers) |
| `quantizations` | string\[] | - | List of quantization levels to filter by (e.g. `["int4", "int8"]`). [Learn more](#quantization) |
| `sort` | string \| object | - | Sort providers by price, throughput, or latency. Can be a string (e.g. `"price"`) or an object with `by` and `partition` fields. [Learn more](#provider-sorting) |
| `preferred_min_throughput` | number \| object | - | Preferred minimum throughput (tokens/sec). Can be a number or an object with percentile cutoffs (p50, p75, p90, p99). [Learn more](#performance-thresholds) |
| `preferred_max_latency` | number \| object | - | Preferred maximum latency (seconds). Can be a number or an object with percentile cutoffs (p50, p75, p90, p99). [Learn more](#performance-thresholds) |
| `max_price` | object | - | The maximum pricing you want to pay for this request. [Learn more](#max-price) |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Regional data residency (Business and Enterprise)**
>
> OpenRouter supports in-region routing in the EU and US on the Business and Enterprise plans. There is no provider preference or setting to turn on: send the request to `https://eu.openrouter.ai` or `https://us.openrouter.ai`, and its prompts and completions are processed entirely within that region. Learn more in the [In-Region Routing guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/in-region-routing.md).

## Default Routing

For each model in your request, OpenRouter picks a provider by comparing what a good response would actually cost you at each one, not by list price alone. Each input is measured from recent production traffic, so routing reacts within minutes when a provider gets faster, slower, or less reliable:

* **Effective price**: the price the provider actually charges, reflecting its real cache hit rate and its typical mix of input and output tokens.
* **Throughput**: end-to-end output tokens per second. A faster provider can charge more and still win your request.
* **Time to first token (TTFT)**: how long you wait before the response starts streaming.
* **Rate limits**: how often the provider rejects requests with a 429 because it is out of capacity.
* **Reliability**: how often requests fail because of the provider.
* **Quality**: whether the provider's tool calls come back well formed.

Providers close to the best share most of the traffic, and each request picks one at random, weighted by those shares. Providers far behind still get a small share, so routing notices when they improve. On top of the shares:

* A provider whose errors or 429s are far worse than the model's other providers gets no traffic until it recovers.
* Routing learns how much load each provider can take before it returns 429s, and sends the rest to other providers.
* A burst of 429s or a jump in latency briefly lowers a provider's share.

If a request fails, the retry is picked the same way from the providers that are left. Follow-up requests in a conversation stay with the same provider while its [prompt cache](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching.md) is warm.

For more detail on each input, see [How OpenRouter Routes Traffic Between Providers](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/providers/traffic-routing.md).

> [!TIP]
>
> When you send a request with `tools` or `tool_choice`, OpenRouter makes a best effort to route to providers known to support tool use. Similarly, if you set `max_output_tokens` (or `max_tokens` on Chat Completions), then OpenRouter will only route to providers that support a response of that length.

Default routing applies whenever you leave the choice of provider to OpenRouter. It is bypassed when you set `sort` (or a default provider sort in your [account settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/preferences)), use the `:floor` or `:nitro` shortcuts, set `order`, or use your own provider key. If you set `only` or `ignore` and two or more providers remain, default routing picks among them.

## Ordering Specific Providers

You can set the providers that OpenRouter will prioritize for your request using the `order` field.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `order` | string\[] | - | List of provider slugs to try in order (e.g. `["anthropic", "openai"]`). |

The router will prioritize providers in this list, and in this order, for the model you're using. The order also outranks the priority your [BYOK keys](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok.md#byok-with-provider-ordering) would otherwise get: within each provider you name, your own key is tried before OpenRouter's shared capacity. If you don't set this field, the router uses [default routing](#default-routing).

> [!TIP]
>
> You can use the copy button next to provider names on model pages to get the exact provider slug, including any variants like "/turbo". See [Targeting Specific Provider Endpoints](#targeting-specific-provider-endpoints) for details.

OpenRouter will try them one at a time and proceed to other providers if none are operational. If you don't want to allow any other providers, you should [disable fallbacks](#disabling-fallbacks) as well.

## Requiring Providers to Support All Parameters

You can restrict requests only to providers that support all parameters in your request using the `require_parameters` field.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `require_parameters` | boolean | `false` | Only use providers that support all parameters in your request. |

With the default routing strategy, providers that don't support all the [LLM parameters](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/parameters.md) specified in your request can still receive the request, but will ignore unknown parameters. ### Default parameter preferences

Even when `require_parameters` is `false`, a small set of parameters is used as a soft preference when choosing between providers of the same model: `tools`, the response format (`text.format` on the Responses API, `response_format` on Chat Completions, including structured outputs), and `verbosity`. ## Requiring Providers to Comply with Data Policies

You can restrict requests only to providers that comply with your data policies using the `data_collection` field.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `data_collection` | "allow" \| "deny" | "allow" | Control whether to use providers that may store data. |

* `allow`: (default) allow providers which store user data non-transiently and may train on it
* `deny`: use only providers which do not collect user data

Some model providers may log prompts, so we display them with a **Data Policy** tag on model pages. This is not a definitive source of third party data policies, but represents our best knowledge.

>

>

## Zero Data Retention Enforcement

You can enforce Zero Data Retention (ZDR) on a per-request basis using the `zdr` parameter, ensuring your request only routes to ZDR endpoints, or to Safety Retention endpoints if your settings allow them.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| `zdr` | boolean | - | Restrict routing to only ZDR (Zero Data Retention) endpoints. |

When `zdr` is set to `true`, the request will only be routed to ZDR endpoints. Safety Retention endpoints (which may retain prompts and responses from any request, only to prevent abuse, and don't train on them) are also eligible unless your privacy settings or guardrail are set to **ZDR only**. See [Allowing or excluding Safety Retention](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zdr.md#allowing-or-excluding-safety-retention). When `zdr` is `false` or not provided, it has no effect on routing.

`zdr` filters model inference endpoints. The [Advisor](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/advisor.md) and [Subagent](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent.md) server tools forward your `provider` preferences, including `zdr`, to their inner generations. > [!TIP]
>

>

The per-request `zdr` parameter operates as an "OR" with your account-wide and guardrail ZDR settings — if any of them is enabled, ZDR enforcement is applied. How CSAM screening will work
How CSAM screening will workScreening also applies to ZDR trafficReporting and preservation requirementsProvider policies may differLooking ahead
OpenRouter will screen all inference requests for child sexual abuse material (CSAM) as they pass through our service. Screening happens in flight, during request processing. Content flagged as potential CSAM may be retained for human review, with reporting and preservation where required by law.
How CSAM screening will work
Known CSAM detection. In-flight screening will include comparing applicable content against hashes (digital fingerprints) of previously identified CSAM.
Review of suspected new CSAM. We may begin retaining content flagged as potential CSAM for human review, including content that does not match a known hash. A flag indicates suspected material; it is not itself a determination that the content is CSAM.
Hash matching detects known material, while classifiers can identify suspected material that has not yet been added to a hash database. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) recommends hashing and image classifiers as basic child-safety measures for services handling images and video, including generative AI services (NCMEC’s guidance).
Screening also applies to ZDR traffic
CSAM screening will also apply to requests covered by OpenRouter’s Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy.
We’re updating our documentation and related terms to make OpenRouter’s own retention commitment explicit:
For inference content covered by OpenRouter’s ZDR policy, we do not retain prompts or responses after processing, except when you explicitly choose to have us store them or when retention is needed for CSAM review, reporting, and related legal preservation.
These CSAM provisions do not authorize general retention of ZDR inference content for unrelated purposes. OpenRouter’s commitment not to use inputs or outputs for model training continues (OpenRouter’s Privacy Policy).
Reporting and preservation requirements
CSAM reporting and preservation duties are established legal obligations. ZDR does not remove those duties.
Under U.S. law, covered providers must report to NCMEC’s CyberTipline as soon as reasonably possible after obtaining actual knowledge of facts or circumstances indicating specified apparent offenses. Reported contents and certain related contextual material must be preserved for one year after submission. That requirement applies to reported material, rather than every item flagged for review (18 U.S.C. § 2258A(a) and (h)).
Provider policies may differ
Model labs and providers may use different screening and retention methods. Some may retain content for a period of time to run automated safety checks before anything has been flagged. Those practices are separate from OpenRouter’s in-flight screening and are governed by the applicable model and provider policies.
OpenRouter documents provider policies so users can understand the requirements that apply to their requests. Review those policies when choosing a model or provider, especially if your organization has specific data-retention requirements.
Looking ahead
AI is opening up exciting possibilities, and the practices surrounding frontier models are evolving quickly. We’re updating our documentation and related terms to describe OpenRouter’s in-flight screening, possible retention of flagged content, and how provider policies are represented. As always, we will keep you informed.

# OpenRouter with `meta/muse-ember` for comment processing

Research for issue #87 (map #85). Researched 2026-11-10 against openrouter.ai (docs, live APIs, model page, terms, DPA), Meta's Model API terms as linked from OpenRouter, and developers.cloudflare.com. No OpenRouter account or API key was used, so nothing below was confirmed by a real request.

**Why it matters.** The product owner chose OpenRouter with `meta/muse-ember` for the Release 2 AI pass over comments, replacing SPEC §10.4's default (Workers AI through AI Gateway, prompt logging off). ADR 0009 says raw comment text is never sent to a model, so only the already-redacted text can be sent. SPEC §7 makes the privacy rules release blockers. The ADR that follows this note has to record the provider, the request settings that enforce no retention, what is sent, and what members are told.

## TL;DR

1. **No zero data retention is possible.** `meta/muse-ember` has exactly one endpoint, served by Meta itself. OpenRouter lists it as `retainsPrompts: true`, `retentionDays: 30`, `training: false`, `is_zdr: false`. It is not in `/api/v1/endpoints/zdr`. With `provider.zdr: true`, or with ZDR enforced on the account or a guardrail, the model has no eligible endpoint and the request fails. No request body can make this model retention-free.
2. **US, not EU.** The model page says "Not currently available through EU in-region routing". The model is missing from both the EU and the US regional model lists. Meta's headquarters is listed as US. OpenRouter publishes no data centre location for Meta (`datacenters: null`, `provider_region: null`).
3. **JSON schema: yes.** The endpoint lists `response_format` and `structured_outputs`. Use `response_format: { type: "json_schema", json_schema: { strict: true, ... } }` on Chat Completions.
4. **Context length is 1,048,576 tokens.** The maximum completion is 943,718 tokens. Reasoning is mandatory (`effort: "none"` is rejected), and the default effort is `max`.
5. **Cost per Round: about $0.001 to $0.003.** Input costs $0.10 per million tokens and output $0.50 per million. One theming call over 20 comments of 300 characters is about 2,500 input and 1,500 to 4,500 output tokens, most of it reasoning. Reasoning tokens are billed as output, so set `reasoning.effort` low and cap `max_tokens`.
6. **A DPA exists and is part of OpenRouter's terms.** It includes Module 2 SCCs and an optional EU-only addendum (Exhibit A). The DPA does not stop Meta keeping prompts: OpenRouter's ZDR promise covers OpenRouter itself, and the provider's own terms govern the provider.
7. **Meta's terms leave a training gap.** Meta's terms split models into "Standard" models (no training) and "Contributor" models (Meta trains on content). Muse Ember was added to OpenRouter on 2026-11-09 and is not on Meta's designation list, which was last updated 2026-10-12. OpenRouter says `training: false`. Meta's own page is silent.
8. **Calling it from a Worker or Durable Object is simple.** Use `fetch` to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions` with the key from a Worker secret, an `AbortSignal.timeout`, and retries on 408/429/502/503 that honour `Retry-After`. Waiting on `fetch` does not count as CPU time.

## 1. The model and its single endpoint

Sources: <https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/meta/muse-ember/endpoints>, the `meta/muse-ember` entry in <https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models>, and the data embedded in <https://openrouter.ai/meta/muse-ember>. All three were read on 2026-11-10.

| Field | Value |
| - | - |
| Canonical slug | `meta/muse-ember-20261109` (created 2026-11-09) |
| Endpoints | **One**: "Meta \| meta/muse-ember-20261109", provider slug `meta`, upstream `https://api.meta.ai/v1` |
| Context length | 1,048,576 tokens. `max_completion_tokens` 943,718 |
| Input modalities | text, image, video, file, audio. Output: text |
| Pricing | prompt $0.0000001/token ($0.10/M), completion $0.0000005/token ($0.50/M), cache read $0.004/M, cache write $0.125/M, web search $0.0025 |
| Supported parameters | `reasoning`, `include_reasoning`, `reasoning_effort`, `max_tokens`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `repetition_penalty`, `tools`, `tool_choice` (only `auto`), `response_format`, `structured_outputs` |
| Reasoning | `mandatory: true`, `default_effort: "max"`, efforts `max`, `xhigh`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `minimal` |
| Moderation | `is_moderated: true`, `moderationRequired: true` |
| Implicit caching | `supports_implicit_caching: false` |
| Quantization | `unknown` |
| Uptime | 100% over 5 min, 30 min and 1 day |

**Latency** (model page, 30-minute window, about 27,500 requests): p50 1.8 s, p75 2.5 s, p90 3.4 s, p95 4.1 s, p99 5.9 s. Throughput p50 157 tokens/s, p99 18 tokens/s. The page labels this metric `latency` without defining it. OpenRouter's [routing docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection.md#default-routing) measure time to first token, so read it as time to first token, not total time. A theming call with a few thousand reasoning tokens will take longer. The model is one day old, so these numbers are early.

**Missing parameters.** `stop`, `seed`, `logprobs` and `frequency_penalty` are not supported. `seed` is missing, so outputs cannot be made reproducible.

## 2. Structured outputs (JSON schema)

Source: <https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/structured-outputs.md>

- On Chat Completions, send `response_format` with `type: "json_schema"` and a `json_schema` object holding `name`, `strict` and `schema`. "The model will respond with a JSON object that strictly follows your schema."
- "Support is determined per endpoint, not just per model." Meta's only endpoint lists both `response_format` and `structured_outputs`, so the schema is enforced on every route this model can take.
- `require_parameters: true` stops OpenRouter from routing to a provider that would silently ignore a parameter ([provider routing](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection.md#requiring-providers-to-support-all-parameters)). With one provider this changes nothing today. It still guards against a second provider being added later without schema support.
- Still decode the reply with Effect Schema. Strict mode limits what the model can emit, but the decode is the boundary check.

## 3. Cost per Round

Assumptions: 20 comments × 300 characters = 6,000 characters, one theming call, a system prompt plus schema of about 800 tokens. The tokenizer is listed only as "Other", so 3 to 4 characters per token is an estimate. German text uses more tokens than English.

| Part | Tokens | Cost |
| - | - | - |
| Input: comments | 1,500 to 2,000 | |
| Input: prompt and schema | about 800 | |
| **Input total** | **about 2,500** | **$0.00025** |
| Output: JSON themes | about 500 | |
| Output: reasoning at `low` or `minimal` effort | about 1,000 to 4,000 (not measured) | |
| **Output total** | **about 1,500 to 4,500** | **$0.00075 to $0.00225** |
| **Per Round** | | **about $0.001 to $0.0025** |

- Reasoning tokens "are considered output tokens and charged accordingly", and on Chat Completions they share the `max_tokens` budget ([reasoning tokens](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/reasoning-tokens.md)). If the budget runs out during reasoning, the reply has `finish_reason: "length"`, empty `content`, and the reasoning is still billed. Treat that as a failure and do not retry it with the same budget.
- The default effort is `max`, "approximately 95% of the limit". **Always send `reasoning.effort`** (`low` or `minimal`) and a `max_tokens` cap. Otherwise one call can produce tens of thousands of output tokens. Even 20,000 tokens is only about $0.01, so the risk is latency and failed calls more than money.
- `reasoning.exclude: true` drops the reasoning text from the reply (Chat Completions only). It is still billed. It keeps model-generated reasoning about member comments out of the response body, so less text needs handling.
- The reasoning token count above is a guess. A spike with an API key should measure it.

## 4. Data policy: Meta, as OpenRouter lists it

Source: the `data_policy` object embedded in <https://openrouter.ai/meta/muse-ember> (identical in the endpoint and provider records), and <https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/providers>.

```json
{
  "training": false,
  "trainingOpenRouter": false,
  "retainsPrompts": true,
  "retentionDays": 30,
  "canPublish": false,
  "safetyRetention": false,
  "termsOfServiceURL": "https://ai.developer.meta.com/legal/terms-of-service",
  "privacyPolicyURL": "https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/",
  "requiresUserIDs": true
}
```

The model page's endpoint stats also carry `"is_zdr": false`.

- **Retention: 30 days.** Meta's endpoint is not in the "Safety Retention" tier (`safetyRetention: false`), so "Allow Safety Retention" (`allow_safety_retention_other`) does not make it eligible either. It falls in the third tier, which the [ZDR guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zdr.md#data-policy-tiers) describes as "data may be stored and used for training under the applicable provider policy", here with training off.
- **ZDR list.** <https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr> held 1,109 endpoints on 2026-11-10. None is `meta/muse-ember`. The Meta-family models on the list are `meta/muse-spark-open` (Makora, Modal, Together, Nebius, BaseTen) and `meta/muse-glimmer-30b` (DeepInfra), all hosted by third parties, not by Meta.
- **`requiresUserIDs: true`.** OpenRouter does not define this flag in its docs. The Chat Completions [`user` field](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/chat/create-a-chat-completion.md) says: "When a provider requires a user identity, OpenRouter folds it into the hashed identity sent upstream and never forwards it raw. If omitted, requests use an account-level identity." So Meta receives a hashed identity on every request. Omitting `user` means that identity is the SurveyBeat account, not a Person.
- **Moderation.** The endpoint is moderated. A flagged input returns `403` with `error.metadata.flagged_input`, "the text segment that was flagged, limited to 100 characters" ([errors](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging.md#moderation-errors)). **An error body can therefore contain comment text.** It must never be logged or stored.
- **How reliable the flags are.** OpenRouter calls the Data Policy tag "not a definitive source of third party data policies, but represents our best knowledge" ([provider routing](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection.md#requiring-providers-to-comply-with-data-policies)). The DPA says the ZDR list "does not constitute OpenRouter's guarantee of AI Model Provider compliance".

## 5. Data policy: Meta's own terms

Source: Meta Model API Terms of Service, last updated 2026-10-09, <https://ai.developer.meta.com/legal/terms-of-service>, and the Model Designation and Geographic Use Policy, last updated 2026-10-12, <https://ai.developer.meta.com/legal/geographic-use-policy>.

- **Two tiers.** "Standard Services": Meta acts as "Service Provider" or "Processor" under the Meta Global Processor Terms (MGPT) and "will not use Content submitted in a request to the Standard Services to train Meta Models" (§5.1). "Contributor Services": "Meta may use your Content to train, develop, evaluate, and improve Meta's artificial intelligence models", and "You must not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information to the Contributor Services" (§6.1, §6.2).
- **Muse Ember is on neither list.** The designation policy lists Standard Models (Muse Image, Muse Spark 1.1 to 1.3, Muse Voice Transcribe, SAM 3.1, Muse Wonder, Muse Wonder Full) and Contributor Models (Muse Spark 1.2 and 1.3 Contributor). Muse Ember is not listed. The terms also say "the system may route you to a Contributor Model, and you are responsible for ensuring that you are accessing and using a Standard or Contributor Model as you intend." Only OpenRouter's `training: false` flag says Ember is not trained on, and OpenRouter does not say which tier its traffic uses or whether it has a separate agreement with Meta. Its [ZDR guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zdr.md#how-openrouter-manages-data-policies) says it "in some cases creates special agreements with providers".
- **Retention for safety, in both tiers.** §4.1: "You instruct Meta to retain and process Content as necessary to detect, prevent, and respond to violations of our Model API AUP … or these Terms and to develop, evaluate, and improve systems for the safety and the security of Meta products and services." §4.4 lists retention "as needed", including "when our systems flag data for a potential policy violation" and "for security, safety, abuse, and policy review and improvements". Meta's terms state no number of days. The 30 days comes only from OpenRouter's flag.
- **Usage Data** (request metadata, timestamps, token counts, latency) may be used by Meta "to test, support, develop, evaluate, and improve" its products (§4.2).
- **Contracting entity.** The terms are with Meta Platforms Ireland Limited for users in the "European Region", otherwise Meta Platforms, Inc. **Where processing happens is not stated.** Through OpenRouter, the contract is with OpenRouter (which accepts the Model Terms on the customer's behalf, see §7), not directly with Meta. Exhibit C ("Hosted Platform") excludes Meta from receiving content only on authorized third-party cloud platforms. OpenRouter's Meta endpoint calls `api.meta.ai` directly, so Exhibit C does not apply.
- The MGPT and Meta's subprocessor list (`forwork.meta.com/legal/mfw-subprocessor-list/`) are linked from the terms. They were not read for this note.

## 6. OpenRouter's own retention and CSAM screening

Sources: <https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/privacy/data-collection.md>, <https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zdr.md#openrouters-retention-policy>, <https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/csam-screening> (2026-10-27).

- "OpenRouter does not store your prompts or responses, *unless* you opt in" to **Private Input & Output Logging** or **OpenRouter Use of Inputs/Outputs** (the 1% discount), "or content is flagged as potential CSAM". Both opt-ins are off by default. Keep them off, and check both settings in every workspace.
- **Metadata is always stored**: token counts, latency and similar, "not … the content of your prompts or responses".
- **Anonymous Input Categorization.** "OpenRouter samples a small number of prompts for categorization … stored completely anonymously and never associated with your account". The categorization runs "by model with a zero-data-retention policy". The docs offer no opt-out. This is content leaving the request path, even if anonymised.
- **CSAM screening** (planned from 2026-10-27, now in the data-collection page): "OpenRouter will screen all inference requests for child sexual abuse material (CSAM) … in flight", "including ZDR traffic". Flagged content "may be retained for human review, reporting, and preservation where required by law". Reported material is preserved for one year under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. For text-only comment theming this is unlikely to trigger, but it is one more documented reason prompts can be kept.
- **DPA §2.4(a).** "Except where required by law or as necessary to address malicious use … OpenRouter will delete Inputs and Outputs promptly following generation of the relevant Output. OpenRouter may apply automated risk classification to Inputs and Outputs prior to deletion."

## 7. Routing controls and the exact request body

Sources: [provider routing](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection.md), [ZDR guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zdr.md), [guardrails](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails.md), [errors](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging.md).

| Control | What it does here |
| - | - |
| `provider.zdr: true` | "the request will only be routed to ZDR endpoints". Muse Ember has none, so the call fails. The 503 meaning, "no available model provider that meets your routing requirements", fits, but the docs do not state the status for this case. ZDR is an OR across request, account and guardrail, so a request cannot turn off ZDR the account enforces. |
| `enforce_zdr_other` (guardrail) / "All other models" toggle (account) | Same effect for every non-Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/SpaceXAI model, Meta included. Enforcing it blocks Muse Ember. |
| `allow_safety_retention_other` | Lets ZDR-enforced requests use Safety Retention endpoints. Meta's endpoint is not Safety Retention, so this does not help. |
| `data_collection: "deny"` | "use only providers which do not collect user data". The field is described as controlling "whether to use providers that may store data", but the bullets talk about training. **The docs do not say whether a 30-day, non-training provider counts as "collecting".** If it does, the call fails like `zdr: true`. Only a real request can tell. |
| `only: ["meta"]` + `allow_fallbacks: false` | Pins the request to Meta's endpoint. With fallbacks off, the request "fails if [the provider] fails" instead of moving to another provider. Today there is no other provider, so this guards against a future one, for example a Contributor or third-party host, being added silently. |
| `require_parameters: true` | Only providers that support every parameter sent, here `response_format` and `reasoning`. |
| No `models` array | A `models` list turns on [model fallbacks](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-fallbacks.md) to other models with other policies. Never send one. |

**Request body.** It enforces no training, no fallback and no OpenRouter-side storage. **It cannot enforce no retention**, because Meta keeps prompts for 30 days on the only endpoint:

```json
{
  "model": "meta/muse-ember",
  "messages": [
    { "role": "system", "content": "<theming instructions; no Organization, Pulse or Round names>" },
    { "role": "user", "content": "<JSON array of already-redacted comment strings, shuffled, no ids>" }
  ],
  "response_format": {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "json_schema": { "name": "themes", "strict": true, "schema": { "...": "..." } }
  },
  "reasoning": { "effort": "low", "exclude": true },
  "max_tokens": 8000,
  "temperature": 0.2,
  "stream": false,
  "provider": {
    "only": ["meta"],
    "allow_fallbacks": false,
    "require_parameters": true,
    "data_collection": "deny"
  }
}
```

- Leave out `user`, `session_id`, `metadata`, `trace` and the `x-session-id` header. Each one sends an identifier upstream or into OpenRouter's observability.
- If the spike shows `data_collection: "deny"` rejects Meta, drop it and rely on the account-level "no training" privacy setting plus `only` and `allow_fallbacks: false`. Record that in the ADR.
- If the ADR requires real no-retention, add `"zdr": true`. The call will fail with this model, so the ADR then needs another model.
- Account settings to set and record: Input & Output Logging off, "OpenRouter Use of Inputs/Outputs" off, training providers excluded for paid models. Use a dedicated API key with a guardrail that allows only `meta/muse-ember` and has a small budget.

## 8. In-region routing

Sources: <https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/in-region-routing.md>, <https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai.md>, the model page.

- EU in-region routing (`https://eu.openrouter.ai`) is on Business and Enterprise plans. The request is "routed only to shared provider endpoints in that region", and "If no endpoint eligible for the region … can serve the request, it errors instead of leaving the region".
- Muse Ember: "Not currently available through EU in-region routing" (model page). `GET /api/v1/models?region=eu` returned 69 models, none of them Muse. `?region=us` returned 134, with `meta/muse-glimmer-30b` but not Muse Ember. **Muse Ember has no regional guarantee in either region.**
- Even on `eu.openrouter.ai`, "Account and operational records" and "Abuse-monitoring metadata" may be stored or processed in the US.

## 9. DPA

Sources: <https://openrouter.ai/data-processing-agreement> (last updated 2026-08-26), <https://openrouter.ai/terms> §10.2.

- **Yes, and it applies by default.** Terms §10.2: for organizations or commercial use, "The DPA is incorporated by reference into, and made a part of, these Terms." No separate signature is needed.
- The customer is Controller and OpenRouter is Processor (§2.1). EEA transfers use Module 2 SCCs, Irish law and Dublin courts (§13.2). There is a UK Addendum and Swiss terms. Breach notice within 72 hours. Deletion of Customer Data on request within 30 business days.
- §2.2: "Customer is responsible for reviewing the data handling terms set forth in AI Model Terms and configuring Customer's account accordingly." **Meta's retention is the customer's problem under the DPA, not OpenRouter's.**
- §5.2: subprocessor-change notices exclude "processing by AI Model Providers". Model providers can change without the 30-day notice.
- **Exhibit A (EU-only processing)** applies only when elected in an Order Form or other written agreement, and only for traffic through the EU API, which routes only to EU Model Providers. It cannot cover Muse Ember, which has no EU endpoint.
- Schedule 1 says "No processing of Sensitive Data or any special categories is intended". Survey comments about a workplace can contain special-category data (health, union membership), and redaction does not remove it.

## 10. Calling from a Worker or Durable Object

Sources: [Workers limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/), [Workers secrets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/secrets/), OpenRouter [errors](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging.md) and [limits](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/limits.md).

- **Transport.** Plain `fetch("https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions", { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: "Bearer " + key, "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body })`. No SDK is needed. The optional `HTTP-Referer` and `X-Title` headers are for attribution only and should be left out.
- **Secret.** Store `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` as a Worker secret, declared in `infra/alchemy.run.ts` like the WorkOS key, and read it from `env`. Only the Worker or Durable Object that runs the theming job gets the binding, never the Submission Worker.
- **CPU and duration.** "Waiting on network requests (such as `fetch()` calls …) does **not** count toward CPU time". Paid CPU defaults to 30 s per request. "There is no hard limit on duration for HTTP-triggered Workers" while the client stays connected. Alarms have 15 min of wall time (see `durable-objects-workflows-limits.md`). Run the call from a Durable Object alarm or a Workflow step, not from the Lead's HTTP request.
- **Timeouts.** OpenRouter documents no server-side request timeout beyond the `408` code. Set your own: `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(60_000)` is generous against a p99 of 5.9 s to first token plus a few thousand reasoning tokens at p99 throughput (18 tokens/s, so about 4 minutes in the worst case). Measure in the spike. Note `isAbortable: false` on Meta's provider record: an aborted request may still run, and may still be billed, upstream.
- **Errors.** A request error has an HTTP status equal to `error.code`. Errors after the model starts can arrive with HTTP **200** and an `error` in the body, so always check the body. Retry `408`, `429`, `502` and `503` with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring `Retry-After` on 429/503. Do not retry `400`, `401`, `402` or `403` (`403` covers moderation flags and budget blocks). Do not retry `finish_reason: "length"` with the same budget. A Workflow step's built-in `retries` (5, exponential) fits.
- **Rate limits.** OpenRouter's published request caps are for `:free` models and key management only. Paid model capacity is "govern[ed] … globally". One call per Round is far below any of them.
- **Logging.** The theming code must not log request bodies, response bodies or error bodies (moderation errors echo up to 100 characters of input). Log the status code, `error.code`, token counts from `usage`, and duration only.

## 11. Where the sources are silent

- Which Meta tier (Standard or Contributor) Muse Ember traffic from OpenRouter uses, and whether OpenRouter has a separate agreement with Meta.
- Where Meta processes requests (country or data centre).
- Whether the 30 days is a fixed deletion deadline, and whether flagged content is kept longer. Meta's terms state no period.
- Whether `data_collection: "deny"` excludes a provider that keeps prompts without training.
- What `requiresUserIDs` sends to Meta beyond "hashed identity".
- The HTTP status for a request that no endpoint can serve under `zdr: true`.
- Real reasoning token counts and total latency for a theming call. These need an API key.

## 12. Open risks for the ADR

1. **This model cannot meet "no retention".** Meta keeps redacted comments for 30 days on its only endpoint, under terms that also allow safety retention for an unstated period. The ADR must either accept retention by a US provider, and say so to members, or choose a ZDR endpoint. Candidates in the ZDR list are `meta/muse-spark-open` on Together, Nebius or Modal, which keeps the Meta model family but uses a third-party host. That choice contradicts SPEC §10.4's data-residency default, so it needs its own ADR, not a silent override.
2. **Training is not settled in Meta's own documents.** OpenRouter says `training: false`. Meta's designation policy does not list Muse Ember, and Meta's terms warn that traffic may be routed to Contributor models. Before launch, get written confirmation (from OpenRouter support or a Meta designation update) that Ember is a Standard model, and re-check the designation page in the ADR's review step.
3. **Redaction is rule-based and imperfect** (ADR 0009). Nicknames, names outside the roster and identifying phrases survive. Whatever survives goes to Meta and stays for 30 days. A 20-comment Round from a small team is easy to re-identify. The minimum group size (ADR 0004) should gate the AI pass too: do not send a Round's comments while fewer than that many Submissions exist.
4. **What may be sent:** only the redacted comment text, as a shuffled JSON array of strings, plus a fixed instruction prompt. **Never send** Person names or ids, emails, Invitation tokens, Edit keys or hashes, Submission or Answer keys, Round ids, Pulse ids or titles, Organization names or ids, timestamps, the order comments arrived in, or attributed/anonymous flags. Do not send `user`, `session_id`, `metadata` or `trace`. Map themes back to comments by array index inside the Durable Object. For anonymous Rounds, ADR 0005's "no time" rule means the call must not reveal submission order, so shuffle before sending.
5. **What members must be told,** on the answer page and the privacy page, before they write: that comments are sent, after the listed redaction, to Meta through OpenRouter (both US companies) to group them into themes; that Meta keeps them for up to 30 days and may keep flagged content longer; that neither uses them for training (subject to risk 2); that processing is not limited to the EU; and that OpenRouter screens requests for CSAM. The current answer-page sentence "Your name is never stored with your answers" stays true, but it is no longer the whole story for comments.
6. **Error bodies carry text.** Moderation `403`s echo up to 100 characters of the flagged input. The theming path needs the same "error codes only" logging rule as the Submission Worker, plus a privacy test that drives a moderation error and asserts that nothing from the body is logged or stored.
7. **The provider can change without notice.** The DPA does not require notice of AI Model Provider changes, and Meta can update its terms and designations at any time. `only` + `allow_fallbacks: false` + `require_parameters: true` stop a new provider being used silently. A scheduled check that `GET /api/v1/models/meta/muse-ember/endpoints` still shows one `meta` endpoint with `training: false` would catch a policy change.
8. **Special-category data.** OpenRouter's DPA says no Sensitive Data processing is intended. Workplace comments can contain it. The ADR should state the lawful basis and whether a DPIA is needed.

The research note is on main: `docs/research/openrouter-muse-ember.md`. PR #96 is squash-merged as `5b571bd1`, the remote branch is deleted, and #87 is still open. I didn't use an API key, so all findings come from reading docs and OpenRouter's public APIs. No request was run against the model.

- **ZDR: no.** `meta/muse-ember` has one endpoint, run by Meta itself. OpenRouter lists it as keeping prompts for 30 days, not training on them, and not ZDR, and it isn't in `/api/v1/endpoints/zdr`. With `provider.zdr: true` (or the account/guardrail setting `enforce_zdr_other`) the request has nowhere to go and fails, so no request body can make this model retention-free.
- **Region: US.** The model page says it isn't available through EU in-region routing, and it's missing from both the EU and the US regional model lists. Meta's headquarters is listed as US, and no source says where Meta processes requests.
- **JSON schema: yes.** The endpoint supports `response_format` with a strict `json_schema`. The context length is 1,048,576 tokens. Reasoning can't be turned off and defaults to `max` effort, so set `reasoning.effort` to low and cap `max_tokens`.
- **Cost per Round: about $0.001–0.0025** for 20 comments of 300 characters in one theming call. Most of the output tokens are reasoning, and that count is a guess until a real call measures it.
- **DPA: yes.** It's part of OpenRouter's terms by default and includes the EU standard contract clauses. It doesn't stop Meta keeping prompts: the DPA puts the provider's terms on the customer, and Meta isn't covered by OpenRouter's no-retention promise.
- **Biggest risk:** members' redacted comments stay with a US provider for 30 days. The training status is also unclear in Meta's own documents. Meta's terms have a no-training "Standard" tier and a tier where Meta trains on content, and Muse Ember isn't on Meta's list of either. Only OpenRouter's flag says it isn't trained on.
- **Other findings:** a moderation error returns up to 100 characters of the comment in its body, so error bodies must never be logged. Whether `data_collection: "deny"` excludes Meta needs a real request to find out.

The note gives the request body that blocks training, fallback to other providers and storage on OpenRouter's side, and states that it can't block Meta's retention. For an ADR that requires real no-retention, the ZDR-eligible alternative is `meta/muse-spark-open`, hosted on Together, Nebius or Modal.

I used plain git instead of GitButler because `but status` here showed the main checkout's workspace, which holds other agents' uncommitted changes. The merge went through while the `check`, `deploy` and `privacy` CI jobs were still pending, because none were required to merge. The change is a single Markdown file, so those jobs shouldn't be affected.
